title: 2  Relations
text:
A relation records which ordered pairs from two sets are related.

Definition 2.1 (Relation) Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be sets. A relation over \(X \times Y\) is a subset \(R \subseteq X \times Y\).
If \(Y=X\), the relation is called homogeneous. When \((x,y)\in R\), we say that \(x\) is related to \(y\) and write \(xRy\).

The definition in Definition 2.1 treats a relation as a set of ordered pairs. Equivalently, its indicator is a proposition-valued function of two arguments.

Example 2.1 (Basic relations) Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be sets. The following are standard examples:

The discrete relation \(X\times Y\).
The empty relation \(\emptyset\subseteq X\times Y\).
When \(Y=X\), the diagonal relation \(\{(x,x):x\in X\}\).



Exercise 2.1 (Equality of the basic relations) Give a necessary and sufficient condition for the empty, discrete, and diagonal relations to be equal.






TipSolution





Assume the three are homogeneous relations on the same set \(X\), so \(Y=X\). They are equal if and only if \(X=\emptyset\).
If \(X=\emptyset\), then
\[
X\times X=\emptyset
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\{(x,x):x\in X\}=\emptyset,
\]
so all three relations coincide. Conversely, if the diagonal relation is empty, then \(X\) has no elements: any \(x\in X\) would make \((x,x)\) an element of the diagonal. Therefore \(X=\emptyset\).





Exercise 2.2 (Product of relations) Let \((X_1,R_1)\) and \((X_2,R_2)\) be pairs of sets and relations on them. The rule
\[
(x,y)\,(R_1\times R_2)\,(x',y')
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
xR_1x'\text{ and }yR_2y'
\]
defines a relation \(R_1\times R_2\) on \(X_1\times X_2\). Express this relation as a subset of \((X_1\times X_2)^2\).






TipSolution





The relation is
\[
R_1\times R_2
=
\left\{
\bigl((x,y),(x',y')\bigr)\in(X_1\times X_2)^2
:
(x,x')\in R_1\text{ and }(y,y')\in R_2
\right\}.
\]

title: 3  Set Identities
text:
This exercise is adapted from Abbott (2015).

Exercise 3.1 (De Morgan’s law for unions) For a sequence of sets \((A_i)_{i=1}^{\infty}\), show that
\[
\left(\bigcup_{i=1}^{\infty} A_i\right)^c
=
\bigcap_{i=1}^{\infty} A_i^c.
\]






TipSolution





We show equality by a chain of biconditionals. For arbitrary \(x\),
\[\begin{align*}
x \in \left(\bigcup_{i=1}^{\infty} A_i\right)^c
&\iff x \notin \bigcup_{i=1}^{\infty} A_i \\
&\iff x \notin A_i \text{ for every } i\in\mathbb N \\
&\iff x \in A_i^c \text{ for every } i\in\mathbb N \\
&\iff x \in \bigcap_{i=1}^{\infty} A_i^c.
\end{align*}\]




This elementwise proof establishes the identity directly.




Abbott, Stephen. 2015. Understanding Analysis. 2nd ed. Springer. https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/978-1-4939-2712-8.

title: 4  Vector Spaces
text:
This exercise is adapted from Axler (2024).

Exercise 4.1 (Double additive inverse) Prove that \(-(-v)=v\) for every \(v\in V\).






TipSolution





Let \(v\in V\). By definition, \(-v\) is an additive inverse of \(v\), so
\[
v+(-v)=0.
\]
Commutativity gives \((-v)+v=0\). But \(-(-v)\) is also defined by
\[
(-v)+(-(-v))=0.
\]
Because additive inverses are unique, \(-(-v)=v\).




The statement only uses the additive-group structure; no scalar multiplication is needed.




Axler, Sheldon. 2024. Linear Algebra Done Right. 4th ed. Undergraduate Texts in Mathematics. Springer. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-41026-0.

title: 5  Convex Sets
text:
These exercises are adapted from Boyd and Vandenberghe (2004).

Exercise 5.1 (Finite convex combinations) Let \(C \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n\) be a convex set, with \(x_1, \ldots, x_k \in C\), and let \(\theta_1, \ldots, \theta_k \in \mathbb{R}\) satisfy
\[
\theta_i \geq 0,
\qquad
\theta_1 + \cdots + \theta_k = 1.
\]
Show that
\[
\theta_1x_1 + \cdots + \theta_kx_k \in C.
\]
The definition of convexity gives this result for \(k=2\); prove it for arbitrary \(k\).
Hint. Use induction on \(k\).






TipSolution





We prove the result by induction on the number of points.
The case \(k=1\) is immediate: the coefficient condition forces \(\theta_1=1\), so \(\theta_1x_1=x_1\in C\).
For the first nontrivial case, let \(k=2\). If \(x_1,x_2\in C\) and \(\theta\in[0,1]\), then the definition of convexity gives
\[
(1-\theta)x_1+\theta x_2\in C.
\]
Thus every convex combination of two points in \(C\) belongs to \(C\).
Now suppose every convex combination of \(\ell\) points in \(C\) belongs to \(C\). In other words, whenever
\[
x_i\in C,
\qquad
\theta_i\geq0,
\qquad
\sum_{i=1}^{\ell}\theta_i=1,
\]
we have
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{\ell}\theta_i x_i\in C.
\]
Let \(x_1,\ldots,x_{\ell+1}\in C\), and let \(\phi_i\geq0\) satisfy
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{\ell+1}\phi_i=1.
\]
If \(\phi_{\ell+1}=1\), then \(\phi_1=\cdots=\phi_\ell=0\), so
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{\ell+1}\phi_i x_i=x_{\ell+1}\in C.
\]
Now suppose \(\phi_{\ell+1}<1\), and define
\[
z=\frac{1}{1-\phi_{\ell+1}}
\sum_{i=1}^{\ell}\phi_i x_i.
\]
Since
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{\ell}\phi_i=1-\phi_{\ell+1},
\]
the coefficients in the definition of \(z\) are nonnegative and sum to one. The induction hypothesis therefore implies that \(z\in C\).
Finally,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{i=1}^{\ell+1}\phi_i x_i
&=\sum_{i=1}^{\ell}\phi_i x_i+\phi_{\ell+1}x_{\ell+1} \\
&=(1-\phi_{\ell+1})z+\phi_{\ell+1}x_{\ell+1}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Because \(z,x_{\ell+1}\in C\) and \(\phi_{\ell+1}\in[0,1]\), convexity of \(C\) gives
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{\ell+1}\phi_i x_i\in C.
\]
Therefore, by induction, every finite convex combination of points in \(C\) belongs to \(C\).





Exercise 5.2 (Distance between parallel hyperplanes) For \(a\neq0\), what is the distance between the parallel hyperplanes
\[
H_1=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n\mid a^Tx=b_1\}
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
H_2=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n\mid a^Tx=b_2\}?
\]






TipSolution





For every \(x_1\in H_1\) and \(x_2\in H_2\),
\[
a^T(x_1-x_2)=b_1-b_2.
\]
The Cauchy–Schwarz inequality therefore gives
\[
|b_1-b_2|
=|a^T(x_1-x_2)|
\leq\lVert a\rVert\,\lVert x_1-x_2\rVert.
\]
Thus every pair of points, one from each hyperplane, satisfies
\[
\lVert x_1-x_2\rVert
\geq
\frac{|b_1-b_2|}{\lVert a\rVert}.
\]
This lower bound is attained. Choose any \(x_2\in H_2\) and define
\[
x_1=x_2+\frac{b_1-b_2}{\lVert a\rVert^2}a.
\]
Then
\[
a^Tx_1
=a^Tx_2+\frac{b_1-b_2}{\lVert a\rVert^2}a^Ta
=b_2+(b_1-b_2)
=b_1,
\]
so \(x_1\in H_1\), and
\[
\lVert x_1-x_2\rVert
=\left\lVert\frac{b_1-b_2}{\lVert a\rVert^2}a\right\rVert
=\frac{|b_1-b_2|}{\lVert a\rVert}.
\]
Hence the distance between the hyperplanes is
\[
\boxed{\frac{|b_1-b_2|}{\lVert a\rVert}}.
\]





Exercise 5.3 (Voronoi description of a halfspace) Let \(a\) and \(b\) be distinct points in \(\mathbb{R}^n\). Show that the set of all points that are closer in Euclidean norm to \(a\) than to \(b\),
\[
\{x\mid \lVert x-a\rVert_2\leq\lVert x-b\rVert_2\},
\]
is a halfspace. Describe it explicitly as an inequality of the form \(c^Tx\leq d\). Draw a picture.






TipSolution





Since both sides are nonnegative,
\[
\lVert x-a\rVert_2\leq\lVert x-b\rVert_2
\iff
\lVert x-a\rVert_2^2\leq\lVert x-b\rVert_2^2.
\]
Expanding the squared norms gives
\[
\lVert x-a\rVert_2^2=x^Tx-2a^Tx+a^Ta,
\qquad
\lVert x-b\rVert_2^2=x^Tx-2b^Tx+b^Tb.
\]
The quadratic terms cancel, leaving
\[
2(b-a)^Tx\leq b^Tb-a^Ta.
\]
Thus
\[
\{x\mid\lVert x-a\rVert_2\leq\lVert x-b\rVert_2\}
=
\{x\mid c^Tx\leq d\},
\]
where
\[
c=b-a,
\qquad
d=\frac{1}{2}\bigl(\lVert b\rVert_2^2-\lVert a\rVert_2^2\bigr).
\]
Since \(a\neq b\), we have \(c\neq0\), so this is a halfspace. Geometrically, its boundary is the perpendicular bisector of the segment \([a,b]\), and the halfspace contains \(a\).








Boyd, Stephen, and Lieven Vandenberghe. 2004. Convex Optimization. Cambridge University Press. https://doi.org/10.1017/CBO9780511804441.
